title_en: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
title_fa: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
excerpt_en: Flox's edge devices can identify animals and use species-specific sounds to drive them away from critical infrastructure.
excerpt_fa: Flox's edge devices can identify animals and use species-specific sounds to drive them away from critical infrastructure.
content_en:
When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet.
The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays.
Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.
“I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch.
After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
“We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.”
So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is.
That work turned into Flox Intelligence, which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.
Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals.
The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones.
Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner.
The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said.
As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed.
Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.”
“Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.”
The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said.
The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases.

title_en: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
title_fa: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
excerpt_en: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe's startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO's secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company's ultimately unsuccessful...
excerpt_fa: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe's startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO's secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company's ultimately unsuccessful...
content_en:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

title_fa: What is NVIDIA DLSS and how does it work?
excerpt_en: NVIDIA's upscaling software is truly powerful when used in the right situations.
excerpt_fa: NVIDIA's upscaling software is truly powerful when used in the right situations.
content_en:
What is NVIDIA DLSS and how does it work?
The company's upscaling software is truly powerful when used in the right situations.
If you own a recent NVIDIA GPU (or Nintendo Switch 2), there's a good chance you bought it partly from hearing good things about DLSS. Short for Deep Learning Super Sampling, DLSS is a proprietary upscaling technology designed to increase game performance. With DLSS enabled, your GPU will first render a game at a lower internal resolution, meaning it will need to draw fewer pixels. DLSS will then upsample the image to your monitor's native resolution using a machine learning algorithm trained by NVIDIA.
When it's implemented well in a game, DLSS allows you to effectively turn up the graphical settings higher than your GPU would normally allow at a native resolution while still getting a playable framerate. Alternatively, you run a game at lower settings and push the framerate even higher, which can be useful if own a high refresh rate monitor.
How does DLSS work?
The above gives a decent starting point for how DLSS works, but knowing a bit more can help with tweaking to get the most out of the tech and your GPU. As mentioned already, with DLSS enabled your GPU will first render a game at a lower resolution before upscaling the image it produces to whatever resolution you've set as the target. In almost every case, you'll want to configure the target resolution to match your monitor's native resolution. So if you own a 1440p monitor, set the output resolution to 1440p. In most games, you do this simply by setting the "display" resolution.
Now comes the more complicated part. DLSS can feel like magic, but ultimately it involves a compromise. The different machine learning models that underpin the tech are trained to interpret motion vectors, as well as depth and brightness information when they upscale an image. Over the years, NVIDIA's GPUs and models have gotten better at doing that, but at the end of the day, some amount of fidelity is lost any time you upscale an image. How much is lost depends on the DLSS mode you use, which determines the internal render (or starting) resolution your GPU has to upscale from:
Quality: When set to Quality mode, your GPU will render a game at 66.7 percent of your target output resolution. For a 4K monitor, that means you're starting with a 1440p image. With a 1440p monitor, your starting point is 960p. DLSS Quality offers the best image quality of the different presets, but expect only a moderate increase in frame rate.
Balanced: When set to Balanced mode, your GPU will render a game at 58 percent of your target output resolution. At 4K, that means a starting point of 1253p. At 1440p, meanwhile, you're upscaling from an 835p image. As the name suggests, Balanced mode is intended to offer a middle ground between image quality and a higher frame rate.
Performance: When set to Performance mode, your GPU will render a game at 50 percent of your target output resolution. That translate to 720p internal resolution when used in conjunction with a 1440p monitor and a 1080p internal resolution when the output is a 4K resolution.
Ultra Performance: When set to Ultra Performance, your GPU will render a game at 33.3 percent of your output resolution. This mode is intended to be used with 8K monitors. Expect a blurry image if used in conjunction with a 1440p or 4K monitor.
As a rule of thumb, if you're running a 1440p monitor, DLSS Quality is a good starting point for most games. If you're not happy with your performance or chasing an even higher frame rate, drop down to Balanced mode. Beyond that, the final image can get quite blurry. For 4K monitors, Balanced mode is a good starting, and then bump things down to Performance if you need or want more frames.
The many different features of DLSS
One of the confusing things about DLSS is that the branding has come to encompass a handful of related technologies that you can use in combination with one another.
Deep Learning Super Sampling: The initial version of DLSS arrived in 2019, following the release of NVIDIA's RTX 20 series GPUs. At launch, only a handful of games supported DLSS, namely Battlefield V and Metro Exodus, due to a limitation that meant NVIDIA had to train the algorithm specifically for the game it was meant to enhance. Since the release of DLSS 2 in 2020, that limitation no longer exists, and according to NVIDIA more than 1,000 games and apps offer DLSS support as of the start of 2025.
Following 2020, the biggest upgrade to DLSS came at the start of 2025 when NVIDIA reworked the algorithm to take advantage of a new transformer-based machine learning architecture and released DLSS 4. The new model offers better image quality, reduced ghosting and improved image stability. On older RTX GPUs, running DLSS 4 can result in worse performance relative to previous versions of DLSS due to a higher overhead. For that reason, NVIDIA gives users access to different DLSS "presets" (separate from the modes described above), which they can use to access older models.
Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing: Where DLSS is primarily designed to increase performance at the cost of image quality, Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing or DLAA does the opposite. Rather than upscaling an image, DLAA takes a native output and makes it more stable by reducing the amount of shimmer and flickering. Think of it a better version of temporal anti-aliasing or TAA. Not every game natively supports DLAA, but even in the ones that don't, you can use the NVIDIA app to add DLAA.
Frame Generation: Originally introduced as part of DLSS 3, frame generation allows NVIDIA RTX 40 series GPUs and up to generate a single interpolated frame from every two traditionally rendered frames, thereby increasing the overall framerate of a game. Frame generation is best used when your GPU can render a game at a consistent 60 FPS or more, and you have a high-refresh rate monitor that will benefit from the extra frames.
With DLSS 4, NVIDIA...

title_en: Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 hands-on: A look at the audio updates and Siri AI
title_fa: Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 hands-on: A look at the audio updates and Siri AI
excerpt_en: Listening to Apple's new audio features with Siri as our binge-watching companion.
excerpt_fa: Listening to Apple's new audio features with Siri as our binge-watching companion.
content_en:
Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 hands-on: A look at the audio updates and Siri AI
Listening to Apple's new sound features with Siri as our binge-watching companion.
Apple's "Welcome home" event may have been mostly for the HomeView debut, but the company also announced updated versions of the HomePod mini speaker and Apple TV 4K. After spending some time with the main attraction this morning, I was also able to check out the HomePod mini 2's revamped home theater features and see Siri AI in action on Apple's streaming box. I also listened to a pair of the new speakers connected to an iMac as part of an enhanced desktop audio setup, and can confirm the new colors match up nicely with the company's all-in-one computer.
Apple TV 4K's Siri overhaul
Let's start with the Apple TV 4K. The main upgrades here are meant to bring Siri AI to the living room, primarily for content discovery. Thanks to the assistant's ability to pull in context from places like Messages, you can ask it to do things like "play the show Sam texted me about." The new Apple TV 4K has far field microphones built in, so the Siri experience is now hands-free, meaning you could shout at it from your couch. This worked well the demo area I was in, though I have to point out the environment was relatively quiet.
Siri AI can also answer questions about content, like whether Ted Lasso is a real person or if AFC Richmond is an actual football club. Thankfully, Siri's responses are tucked in the corner of the TV screen, so you can see them without the text blocking your movie or show. What's more, they're text only, and the assistant won't respond to you by speaking over the audio from whatever you're watching. I saw this in action a few different times, and I think it's a clean implementation of Siri on the Apple TV 4K. I really like that I won't have to hear competing sounds from Siri and a TV show, forcing me to try to decipher the info I asked for.
Another welcome upgrade for the Apple TV 4K is an overhauled remote. While it looks the same on the outside, a new feature inside will play a sound when you ask Siri for help finding it. I prefer this approach since it's much quicker to determine where something is if it's beeping than having to wave a phone around to see how close I'm getting to it. If you've ever played a sound to find your AirPods, that works the same way. I'm constantly looking for my Apple TV remote after one of my kids has stashed it somewhere, so this will all be handy at my house.
Audio updates on the HomePod mini 2
The HomePod mini 2 has also been updated for Siri AI. Right off the top, the speaker is now powered by the S10 chip, a big upgrade over the S5 that was in the 2020 model. This hardware will eventually enable Siri AI, but the next-gen — or now current-gen — assistant won't be on the HomePod mini 2 at launch. Apple says that feature is coming at a later date.
For now, the two big new features are Sound Glow and expanded surround sound functionality. Sound Glow mimics album artwork on the HomePod mini 2's back-lit touch panel. If you're listening to a soundscape, the lights will mirror things like rain drops and waves. This is a neat addition, but I wonder how often I'll actually see it since I don't tend to sit near or even look at my HomePod speakers. Next, you can now use up to four HomePod speakers with the new Apple TV 4K for home theater audio. Before, you could only use two as a stereo pair.
After hearing two different configurations at Apple's event, I'm convinced this is going to be an audio upgrade for those willing to buy four HomePods. I enjoyed the setup of two second-gen HomePods in the front and two HomePod mini 2 speakers in the back as it offered more bass and rumble during my demo. However, a quartet of HomePod mini 2 speakers holds its own, providing dimensional sound that enveloped the sofa I was sitting on. But again, this is all dependent upon you buying four HomePods and putting them all in your living room, which seems like a rare scenario.
Lastly, I got to hear a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers being used for audio from an iMac. These new speakers can sync with any Mac over AirPlay to function as a set of desktop speakers. This setup provides an obvious upgrade over built-in iMac speakers, and the stereo pair offered solid directional sound for basic games like Angry Birds. At around $300 for two of the HomePod mini 2, this seems like a more plausible arrangement than the four-pack in the living room.

title_en: Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot gets a full series order from Hulu
title_fa: Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot gets a full series order from Hulu
excerpt_en: It stars two new FBI agents that aren't named Mulder and Scully.
excerpt_fa: It stars two new FBI agents that aren't named Mulder and Scully.
content_en:
Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot gets a full series order from Hulu
It stars Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel as two new FBI agents that aren't named Mulder and Scully.
Hulu has officially picked up Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot, after greenlighting a pilot back in February. Variety reports that Coogler wrote and directed the pilot, fresh off of Sinners, and will stay on as an executive producer for the rest of the episodes.
We don't know much about the plot here, though Coogler has made comments that suggest this is a sequel series of some kind and not a total reboot. He has called it a "new chapter" and that the team "wanted to honor everything that made the original series connect with so many people while also finding our own way into that world."
Both a reboot and a sequel series have their risks. X-Files was on for 11 seasons in total, with an absolutely nutty mythology that nobody in their right mind would be expected to remember. However, people tend to resent total reboots of properties that are highly beloved and aired in most peoples' living memory.
We do know that the show stars Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel as two FBI agents who are not named Mulder and Scully. Their characters have been described as "two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents" that "form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena." That certainly sounds like X-Files to me.
Jennifer Yale is the showrunner, and not Coogler. She's written for shows like Legion, See, Dexter and Your Friends & Neighbors, among many others.
This pilot getting picked up for a full series order wasn't a given, despite the name recognition of Coogler and the X-Files IP. Hulu also greenlit a pilot for a Buffy the Vampire Slayer sequel series, which was helmed by Oscar-winning director Chloé Zhao. The platform eventually passed on that one, which is a bummer.

title_en: Don't like your Facebook feed? Meta wants to know what you want to see instead
title_fa: Don't like your Facebook feed? Meta wants to know what you want to see instead
excerpt_en: Within reason, of course.
excerpt_fa: Within reason, of course.
content_en:
Don't like your Facebook feed? Meta wants to know what you want to see instead
The company is using LLMs for algorithm personalization.
If you've ever scrolled through your Facebook feed and wondered why you're suddenly flooded with weird AI-generated celeb bait and posts from cast iron pan enthusiasts (just me?), Meta has a new tool that might help. The company is rolling out a new algorithm personalization feature that aims to make it easier for users to explain exactly what they do and don't want to see in their recommendations.
With the update, you can dive into specific feed posts and Reels to access a new "your algorithm" menu. From there, you can add specific topics to your interests and to your "not interested in" list. There's also a box where Meta prompts you to describe in your own words what you want to see in your feed.
The update mirrors a similar change that landed on Instagram earlier this year. The update is possible, Meta says, because it now uses large language models in its ranking systems. Instead of simply "inferring what you're into from what you engage with on Facebook," the company explains, "LLMs can incorporate the interests, context, and intent behind natural language, unlocking an algorithm you can actually talk to."
The change has yet to roll out on my app, so I haven't been able to try it yet. The Instagram version of the feature had some limitations, though. It didn't allow me to add "posts from people I follow" as one of my interests or request fewer ads. Given Meta's previous efforts to clean up the amount of spam and engagement bait in the Facebook feed, I am curious whether users will be able to request more holistic changes, like "less AI-generated content" or "no more Reddit copypasta." At the very least, I am looking forward to finally telling Facebook that I actually have no special interest in cast iron pans.

title_en: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
title_fa: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
excerpt_en: Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” a feature it first launched on Instagram.
excerpt_fa: Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” a feature it first launched on Instagram.
content_en:
Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds.
Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.
According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.
The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences.
Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.
The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.
The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025.
Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them.

Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.
According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.
The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences.
Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.
The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.
The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025.
Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them.

title_en: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
title_fa: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
excerpt_en: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality.
excerpt_fa: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality.
content_en:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.
There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.)
And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space.
Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.
When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.
The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.
The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.
These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)
“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”
The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.
“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.
But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.
It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.
If you want to learn more about Longshot from the company itself — while also checking out dozens of startups, hearing their pitches, and listening to guest speakers on four different stages — join us this week at Disrupt, Tuesday to Thursday, in San Francisco. Learn more here.

content_en:
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
The Good
- I don’t feel like a creep wearing these
- Long battery life
- Lightweight
- Stylish
- Good for open-ear audio
The Bad
- Expensive for what they are
- Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently...

title_en: Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses review: No camera, no problem
title_fa: Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses review: No camera, no problem
excerpt_en: Normal-looking glasses with solid audio and way better battery life is a win for everyone.
excerpt_fa: Normal-looking glasses with solid audio and way better battery life is a win for everyone.
content_en:
Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses review: No camera, no problem
Normal-looking glasses with solid audio and way better battery life is a win for everyone.
Meta's audio-only smart glasses couldn't have come at a more opportune time. At a moment when there's increasing backlash against the company's growing lineup of camera-enabled glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio frames ditch the feature most associated with "creep glasses." Instead, as the name implies, the frames are all about making the most of audio.
The result is a pair of glasses that are lighter, more comfortable and have far better battery life than any other glasses from the company. They also look a lot more subtle and are the closest to "normal" glasses we've seen from Meta.
New style, better fit
Meta has two different frame styles for its $349 audio-only glasses: Burbank, which looks a bit like a thinner Wayfarer, and Clubmaster, an immediately recognizable Ray-Ban design. I opted for the latter because it comes in a wider variety of colors and I prefer thinner frames in general.
From the front, I'm not sure anyone would recognize the glasses as having any tech abilities. My frames did have the transparent arms Meta often uses to display the inner circuitry of the glasses, but it's still relatively subtle.
There isn't a camera or front-facing LED, but the setup is overall similar to Meta's other glasses. The right arm still has a touchpad for controlling volume, answering calls and other functions, and there's a small inward-facing LED for notifications. There's also a tiny action button, which you can use as a dedicated shortcut for certain features.
It might seem like Meta simply stripped down its existing glasses designs, but the company's VP of Wearables, Ming Hua, told me that the company actually had to rebuild the speaker and microphone setup to work on a smaller frame.
That work definitely paid off. The audio-only glasses are noticeably slimmer than other models. They also fit better and are far more comfortable because less of the weight sits toward the front of the frames. At 47 grams, the Clubmaster glasses are only 2 grams lighter than the Ray-Ban Meta Optics frames, but they feel significantly lighter because they put less pressure around my nose.
If you've read my past reviews of other Meta-branded glasses, you know I often struggle with getting a good fit. Most of the frame styles feel like they are meant for faces just a bit wider than my own, and the weight tends to cause them to slip around my face.
But the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have traditional notepads that actually stay in place. You can also get the tips adjusted by an optician (Meta also provides this service at its retail stores and pop-ups as well), but these actually fit me well out of the box without any tweaks. I wore them for several long stretches and actually forgot I was wearing smart glasses because they felt so much like my typical shades.
No camera, (mostly) the same AI
Like other recent glasses from Meta, the audio-only frames have 6 mics and open-ear speakers. Music, podcasts and phone calls sounded just as good as my Gen 2 glasses. One quirk of the audio-only glasses is that the microphones are in slightly different places. There are now two mics on the front of the frames, replacing the ones that were embedded in the nosepads in previous models. The other four are on the arms. This new placement didn't seem to affect things, though. Friends and family told me I sounded clearer on calls when I was wearing the audio glasses, compared with my second-gen AirPods Pro.
The other major advantage the audio-only glasses have compared with other models is the battery life. Meta says the frames can go 12 hours on a charge with "mixed use" and up to six hours of continuous audio playback. I haven't done a full battery rundown, but I still had close to 50 percent battery after five hours of streaming audio and a one-hour phone call. If you aren't listening to hours of music or podcasts, the glasses will easily go all day without needing to recharge.
Even though there's no camera, you can still use most Meta AI features, including live translation and walking navigation. Meta is also planning to bring its AI agent, Muse, to its glasses, so the audio frames will also be a conduit to your personal agent once that update rolls out. (The company has said to expect it in the "coming months.")
One thing that did frustrate me about Meta's implementation of its assistant on the audio-only glasses is that the action button is so limited. On other frames that have the control (Meta Glasses, Oakley Meta Vanguard sunglasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Optics line, and Gen 3 Ray-Ban Meta frames), there are quite a few options for what that shortcut can trigger. Some of these are related to the camera, but many others aren't, like call muting or playing music.
But on the audio-only frames, there are only two options for what this button can do. If you select "music," it will play recommended playlists, or you can set it as a shortcut to activate Meta AI. The latter is useful if you don't enjoy saying "Hey Meta" in public, but you can't set it to trigger a specific prompt like you can on other glasses. You also can't use the button to answer or mute calls, both of which could be useful shortcuts for audio-only glasses.
It's an annoying limitation and I don't understand why Meta would limit what the only button on the glasses could do. The good news, though, is that this is likely something that can be addressed in future software updates, so I'm hopeful we might get a little more functionality out of the action button in time.
Does ditching the camera solve the privacy issues?
When I was interviewing Meta glasses users earlier this year about how the privacy backlash has affected how they use the product, a lot of people told me they loved their glasses, but were worried about how others might perceive them. Some said they would happily buy a pair without cameras if it would...

Like other recent glasses from Meta, the audio-only frames have 6 mics and open-ear speakers. Music, podcasts and phone calls sounded just as good as my Gen 2 glasses. One quirk of the audio-only glasses is that the microphones are in slightly different places. There are now two mics on the front of the frames, replacing the ones that were embedded in the nosepads in previous models. The other four are on the arms. This new placement didn't seem to affect things, though. Friends and family told me I sounded clearer on calls when I was wearing the audio glasses, compared with my second-gen AirPods Pro.
The other major advantage the audio-only glasses have compared with other models is the battery life. Meta says the frames can go 12 hours on a charge with "mixed use" and up to six hours of continuous audio playback. I haven't done a full battery rundown, but I still had close to 50 percent battery after five hours of streaming audio and a one-hour phone call. If you aren't listening to hours of music or podcasts, the glasses will easily go all day without needing to recharge.
Even though there's no camera, you can still use most Meta AI features, including live translation and walking navigation. Meta is also planning to bring its AI agent, Muse, to its glasses, so the audio frames will also be a conduit to your personal agent once that update rolls out. (The company has said to expect it in the "coming months.")
One thing that did frustrate me about Meta's implementation of its assistant on the audio-only glasses is that the action button is so limited. On other frames that have the control (Meta Glasses, Oakley Meta Vanguard sunglasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Optics line, and Gen 3 Ray-Ban Meta frames), there are quite a few options for what that shortcut can trigger. Some of these are related to the camera, but many others aren't, like call muting or playing music.
But on the audio-only frames, there are only two options for what this button can do. If you select "music," it will play recommended playlists, or you can set it as a shortcut to activate Meta AI. The latter is useful if you don't enjoy saying "Hey Meta" in public, but you can't set it to trigger a specific prompt like you can on other glasses. You also can't use the button to answer or mute calls, both of which could be useful shortcuts for audio-only glasses.
It's an annoying limitation and I don't understand why Meta would limit what the only button on the glasses could do. The good news, though, is that this is likely something that can be addressed in future software updates, so I'm hopeful we might get a little more functionality out of the action button in time.
Does ditching the camera solve the privacy issues?
When I was interviewing Meta glasses users earlier this year about how the privacy backlash has affected how they use the product, a lot of people told me they loved their glasses, but were worried about how others might perceive them. Some said they would happily buy a pair without cameras if it would...

title_en: How the iPhone Duo's camera is different from the iPhone 18 Pro's
title_fa: How the iPhone Duo's camera is different from the iPhone 18 Pro's
excerpt_en: Going beyond the number of cameras and megapixels.
excerpt_fa: Going beyond the number of cameras and megapixels.
content_en:
How the iPhone Duo's camera is different from the iPhone 18 Pro's
Going beyond the number of cameras and megapixels.
The iPhone Duo has by far the highest starting price of any iPhone to date. Which makes sense in a way, since it's basically two devices in one. But at $1,999, it still lacks the iPhone 18 Pro's more advanced camera hardware. A telephoto lens and variable aperture are out, while tricks that take advantage of its foldable design are in. Most of the differences exist due to the limitations and benefits of any dual-screen phone, including challenges around squeezing more cameras into an already crowded device and being able to use an external display for more content. Here's exactly what your photography gives up (and gains) if you choose the Duo over the iPhone 18 Pro.
Fewer cameras, shorter range
Sensor resolution isn't where the iPhone Duo loses ground. It has two 48-megapixel rear cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide, which also handles macro shots. But camera count is another story, as Apple does not offer the telephoto camera on the Duo.
With their high resolution, both phones offer a 2x view by cropping into their 48MP main sensors. But the iPhone 18 Pro has a dedicated 4x telephoto camera, which can also crop its 48MP sensor to make a 12MP "optical quality" 8x zoomed shot. The best the Duo can do is 2x optical-quality zoom.
In practice, that means the iPhone Duo probably won't be a great choice for shooting distant subjects like a performer on a concert stage or athlete at a sporting event. Sure, you can use digital zoom to go past that "optical" limit, but quality will suffer the farther you go past 2x.
Why would Apple leave something as basic as a telephoto lens out of its first $2,000 iPhone? Well, the company hasn't said, but it may be as simple as physical constraints. Since a foldable phone opens into a bigger device, its cameras have to fit into one very thin half. Camera modules also have to compete with other hardware (especially batteries) for extremely limited internal space.
That doesn't mean future versions of the Duo won't get a dedicated zoom lens. After all, other foldable manufacturers have managed to squeeze one in. And it leaves at least one obvious place for Apple to entice upgraders with sequels.
Another big omission is variable aperture, which is one of the iPhone 18 Pro's headline features. It can physically widen or narrow its opening, adjusting how much light enters (and how much of the scene stays in focus). The Duo's aperture is fixed, just like on all previous iPhones. It still supports portrait-mode background blur, but that digital effect isn't the same.
The Duo's unique tricks
Since the Duo can stay upright and basically prop itself up when partially folded, its camera can take advantage of this faux built-in tripod. This makes it an interesting choice for things like group photos and video calls.
The Duo has a 12MP selfie camera on its outer screen, along with a separate 1080p FaceTime camera hidden beneath the inner folding display. The outer screen can also act as a viewfinder for the higher-resolution 48MP rear cameras, and if you open the Duo all the way, you can point those cameras at your face while still seeing what's in the shot. Perfect for high-res selfies.
You can also set it down somewhere and join the shot while using the outer screen to check the framing. Traditional slab-like iPhones can't do that.
A Duo-specific feature called Smart Take goes a step further: it recognizes when everyone in a group photo is ready and takes the photo automatically.
The Duo also has a trick for video calls: Duo FaceTime lets someone around you join the call using the outer display and camera, rather than crowding next to you for the inner screen. Then there's Kid Cue, which shows Peanuts animations on the outer display to get kids to look toward the phone.
So, it's not that the Duo's camera setup is without its own unique (if quirkier) perks. It's just that the iPhone 18 Pro provides the more complete and traditional camera experience.
The iPhone 18 Pro's other advantages
The two still have plenty of overlap. Both support 24MP and 48MP photos, adjustable portraits and updated Photographic Styles, including texture and grain adjustments. They can each record in 4K Dolby Vision at up to 120 fps, and both let you apply Cinematic effects after the fact.
But the Pro's advantages become clearer when you want to take over from the phone's automatic settings. Thanks to the new variable aperture, the Pro offers, well, Pro Controls, which are manual adjustments for things like shutter speed, white balance and aperture. The Duo doesn't offer that.
The Duo also lacks ProRAW photos, which preserve extra sensor data for advanced editing in apps like Lightroom. Video gets shorted, too: there's no ProRes, ProRes RAW or Apple Log 2 for more flexibility in post-production. Of course, those features will be missed by those who are into fine-tuning professional-class shots with professional-class tools. But if your photography doesn't go much farther than selfies and capturing the dog doing something funny? Well, you probably won't miss them.
Other features are also MIA. The iPhone 18 Pro has second-generation sensor-shift stabilization (the Duo uses the older version), an Adaptive True Tone flash (the Duo's isn't adaptive) and a studio-quality four-microphone array. The Duo also can't record spatial photos or videos, and it lacks Apple's new Reference Image feature, which captures signed sensor data alongside the photo to verify what the camera originally saw.
So, the iPhone 18 Pro is better if you want to shoot distant subjects, more advanced manual control or edits or the more all-around capable camera system.
With cameras that are a step down in several ways, the Duo isn't simply an iPhone 18 Pro that folds. For $2,000 and up, that might be a hard pill to swallow. If you're forking that over, it's probably because you like the folding design and have...

title_fa: The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
excerpt_en: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it's evaluating allegations that Tesla's 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding "posted speed limits in active school zones." Waymo's robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including...
excerpt_fa: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it's evaluating allegations that Tesla's 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding "posted speed limits in active school zones." Waymo's robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including...
content_en:
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school.
The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.
NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.
NHTSA:
The Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) received a DP on September 23, 2026, requesting an investigation into model year (MY) 2026 Tesla Robotaxis (Model Y and Cybercab) with the Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged. The Petitioner alleges that the ADS exceeds posted speed limits in active school zones.
The Cybercab launched earlier this year, and is already under investigation for its lack of side mirrors, pedals, and a steering wheel. NHTSA has also opened an investigation into Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system for traffic violations, like blowing past red lights and driving on the wrong side of the street.

title_en: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
title_fa: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
excerpt_en: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment. The profitable startup is competing in Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 in San Francisco.
excerpt_fa: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment. The profitable startup is competing in Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 in San Francisco.
content_en:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Japanese trucking manufacturer Isuzu and Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto.
Nvidia is also a customer, says Sun. The two companies, alongside T-Mobile, are working together on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Isuzu is also one of Applied’s customers.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new...

title_en: GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
title_fa: GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
excerpt_en: That would be a much smaller port time than GTA 5.
excerpt_fa: That would be a much smaller port time than GTA 5.
content_en:
GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
PC players might be able to dive into Jason and Lucia's story by the end of March.
PC players may not have to wait too much longer to jump into Grand Theft Auto 6. According to GamesBeat's sources, Rockstar Games' upcoming blockbuster will hit PC in the first quarter of 2027, just a few months after its debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19.
That's a much shorter window than Grand Theft Auto 5's initial release on consoles and its arrival on PC. The previous game in the series made its debut on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on September 17, 2013. It didn't come to PC until April 2015.
Most other developers and publishers have given GTA 6 a wide berth this fall, as it's all but guaranteed to be a massive hit that captures the attention of many players. It could well be the case that games that were supposed to arrive early next year end up being delayed to avoid competing with the PC port as well. The release slate for the first quarter of 2027 currently includes Stranger Than Heaven, Metroid Ravenous, Until Dawn 2, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, God of War Laufey and Fable.
It's not clear when Rockstar will add the inevitable online mode (about which it's been tight-lipped) to GTA 6 either. However, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has claimed that'll happen next year. For what it's worth, the hugely popular GTA 5 roleplaying mods are PC-only. Rockstar recently added a GTA 5 roleplaying option to its PC launcher, three years after it acquired the team behind roleplaying server company FiveM. Connecting the dots here, the company may be waiting until it releases the PC version of GTA 6 before it switches on multiplayer.

title_en: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
title_fa: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
excerpt_en: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
excerpt_fa: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
content_en:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

title_en: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
title_fa: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
excerpt_en: Diesel is expensive and polluting, and LNK Energies says it has come up with a way to replace it with hydrogen, all while undercutting diesel on cost.
excerpt_fa: Diesel is expensive and polluting, and LNK Energies says it has come up with a way to replace it with hydrogen, all while undercutting diesel on cost.
content_en:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout.
For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.
LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)
Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly.
LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.
“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”
Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch.
In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.
The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”
Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck.
The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.
LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.
